entry.title: After the midterms: the new Congress, and what happens between now and January
entry.summary: Two days on, Democrats hold 54 Senate seats and are headed for about 259 in the House. Here is the full map of both chambers, the lame-duck deadlines before the handoff, and the race to lead each party, starting with Speaker-in-waiting Hakeem Jeffries.
entry.content:
Two days after the election, the outcome is settled and the margins are still moving. Democrats have clinched the Senate with 54 seats and lead the House with 242 called seats against 151. Forty-two House races and two Senate races are still being counted.12 This follow-up to Wednesday’s results post covers three things: what both chambers will look like in January, what the outgoing Republican Congress still has to do before then, and who will run each party in the 120th Congress.

Chamber Today (119th Congress) Called as of Nov. 5, 10 AM ET Projected for January (120th)
Senate (100) 53 R, 47 D 54 D, 44 R, 2 uncalled 54 to 56 D, depending on Alaska and Mississippi
House (435) 219 R, 214 D, 2 vacant 242 D, 151 R, 42 uncalled NBC estimate: 259 D, 176 R

Every number here is unofficial. States certify over the next few weeks, and each chamber is the final judge of its own members’ elections.3

The full map: the Senate

Wednesday’s map showed only the 35 seats on the ballot. This one shows all 100: each state’s two senators as they will stand when the new Congress meets.

The flips turned eight states into split delegations: Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas now each have one senator from each party, joining Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Maine goes from split to two members of the Democratic caucus: Troy Jackson plus independent Angus King. Two seats, both now held by Republicans, are still in doubt.1

Mississippi: the lead grew, and the count isn’t over. On Wednesday morning Scott Colom (D) led Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 43 votes. By the end of counting Wednesday it was 1,138: 464,926 (49.0 percent) to 463,788 (48.9), with independent Ty Pinkins at 19,934 and about 96 percent of the expected vote in.45 Twelve counties, mostly around Jackson and Gulfport, are still reporting. The secretary of state counts about 3,600 mail ballots that can still arrive. They count if postmarked by Election Day and received by 5 PM on Nov. 10. Voters with affidavit (provisional) ballots have until Nov. 10 to fix problems, and nobody knows how many there are. Colom’s campaign estimates 15,000, and the state says it has no definitive number. Counties must certify by Nov. 13.64

Mississippi has no recount. Candidates can’t request one, and no margin triggers one automatically. A candidate can examine ballot boxes county by county after certification and go to court if they find problems. An Ole Miss election-law attorney told NBC that across 82 counties “that’s beyond the scope of feasibility.”46 Hyde-Smith’s campaign says a full count will reelect her. Colom says he is prepared to litigate.

Alaska: ranked choice decides it. With about three-quarters of the vote in, Mary Peltola (D) led Sen. Dan Sullivan by just over 600 first-choice votes, 48.2 to 47.9 percent.71 Mail ballots from remote areas can arrive up to 15 days after Election Day. If no one reaches a majority, the last-place candidates are eliminated and their ballots move to voters’ next choices. That tabulation is scheduled for Nov. 18, with certification on Nov. 25.8 On Thursday morning President Trump posted that votes for the “Fake Dan Sullivan,” the unrelated candidate with the same name, “should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan.” No court or election official has acted on that.7

Kansas’s governor race is also still open. Cindy Holscher (D) led Ty Masterson by more than 7,000 votes with 99 percent in.7

The full map: the House

By NBC’s tally, Democrats have flipped 35 Republican-held seats and lost one, a net gain of 34 so far. NBC’s model projects 259 Democratic seats, an 83-seat majority, and at least 258.2 For comparison, Republicans won 220 seats in 2024. Some of the trade press is already calling it a “blue tsunami.”9

Since Wednesday’s post, the AP called Michigan’s 10th for Democrat Christina Hines, a flip, over Mike Bouchard.10 Most of the 42 uncalled seats are in states that count mail ballots for days: California, Arizona, Florida, New York, Colorado and Washington. Those states will decide whether the final number lands closer to 250 or 265.

The lame duck: what the outgoing Congress still has to do

Republicans still control both chambers until noon on Jan. 3. Congress returns for its lame-duck session on Nov. 9 and is expected to work until Christmas, with a Thanksgiving break.11 Most of what it has to do runs into two dates:

Deadline What expires Notes
Dec. 11 Government funding (the stopgap signed Sept. 2) The only true hard deadline. Miss it and the government shuts down.2211
Dec. 11 Surface transportation programs, the National Flood Insurance Program Riding on the same stopgap2212
Dec. 31 Community Health Center Fund About 70 percent of federal grant money for health centers22
Dec. 31 Medicare’s temporary 2.5 percent physician pay bump; National Health Service Corps; special diabetes programs Part of a year-end health “extenders” package22
Dec. 31 Farm programs Without action, some revert to “permanent law” from the 1930s and 1940s. The 2018 farm bill lapsed Sept. 3011
Dec. 31 Export-Import Bank charter 12
No date Annual defense bill (NDAA) Passed 65 years running. Stuck on Iran-war oversight and a requested $1.5 trillion defense topline221112
Early 2027 Debt limit Could be reached as soon as February 2027. Majority Leader John Thune has said an increase could come in the lame duck11

The big question is how much gets done now and how much waits for January. Each side has reasons to wait or to move:

  • Republicans’ incentives: This is their last month with the gavels. Expect a push to confirm President Trump’s nominees, including several at Health and Human Services, before Democrats take over the Senate and its confirmation calendar.21 Some Republicans have floated a third budget-reconciliation package that would raise the debt limit for the rest of Trump’s term and add defense money. No package is settled, and some GOP aides expect it to slip to January.1211
  • Democrats’ incentives: In January they will hold both chambers, so they have less reason to strike broad deals now.12 Before the election, Jeffries said he favored finishing the full-year spending bills in the lame duck rather than punting them.22 Whether he still feels that way with an 80-plus-seat majority waiting is one of the first things to watch next week.

The pre-election analyses disagree on the outcome. Congress could pass another short-term funding bill that hands the fight to the new Congress, or it could finish full-year bills now, with a health extenders package riding on either.1112

The new Congress: who runs what

The calendar.

  • Nov. 9: Lame-duck session begins.11
  • Nov. 10: Republican leadership elections in both chambers. Senate Republicans meet at 9 AM in the Old Senate Chamber. House Republicans hold a two-hour candidate forum that morning and vote that afternoon for leader, whip and conference chair.23 Mississippi’s mail-ballot and affidavit deadlines fall the same day.
  • Nov. 13: Mississippi counties certify.6
  • Nov. 18 and 25: Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation, then certification.8
  • Dec. 11: Government funding runs out.
  • Jan. 3, 2027, noon: The 120th Congress convenes, as the 20th Amendment requires unless Congress sets another day by law. Jan. 3 is a Sunday this time, so a law moving the date is possible.3 The House’s first order of business is electing a Speaker.

Speaker of the House: Hakeem Jeffries. The Brooklyn Democrat has led House Democrats since 2023 and is expected to be the next Speaker. He would be the first Black Speaker in U.S. history.13 The formal steps: House Democrats nominate him in a closed caucus vote (we haven’t seen a date announced as of Thursday), and then on Jan. 3 the full House votes by roll call, every member saying a name aloud. The winner needs a majority of those voting for a person. With roughly 259 Democrats, Jeffries could lose dozens of votes and still win on the first ballot. That’s a big change from the two most recent Speaker fights: Kevin McCarthy’s 15-ballot election in 2023 and Mike Johnson’s narrow first-ballot win in 2025. No Democrat has said publicly they will challenge him. Katherine Clark, now the Democratic whip, is expected to stay in senior leadership. Who fills the No. 2 and No. 3 jobs under a Speaker Jeffries hasn’t been reported yet.13

House Republicans: Mike Johnson steps back. Johnson told staff on election night that he won’t run for minority leader.14 Candidates had until noon Nov. 6 to declare.15 Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio and Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana are the names most often reported, but as of Thursday morning neither had formally announced. President Trump said of the race, “We’ll stay out of it.”15 The vote is Nov. 10.

The Senate: Schumer back to majority leader. Chuck Schumer is expected to become majority leader again, swapping places with John Thune.13 Democrats also need a new No. 2. Whip Dick Durbin is retiring, and Juliana Stratton won his Illinois seat on Tuesday.16 Brian Schatz of Hawaii, now chief deputy whip, has Schumer’s endorsement for whip and was reported in 2025 to have locked up the votes.1718

On the Republican side, Thune’s office says he will run for minority leader, and no one has publicly challenged him. Rick Scott said in September he would not run against him again. Whip John Barrasso is expected to stay No. 2, James Lankford to seek another term as conference vice chair, and Shelley Moore Capito to stay Policy Committee chair.19

What divided government looks like from here. For the last two years of Trump’s term, Democrats will control what comes to the floor, the committee gavels and subpoenas, and the Senate’s confirmation calendar. The president keeps the veto and executive action. K&L Gates summed it up the day after the election: Democrats “can thwart the Administration’s priorities, conduct investigations, and advance their own legislative agenda,” while Trump “will continue to act through Executive Action” and “will be able to use his veto power.”20 No Democratic bill becomes law without either Trump’s signature or two-thirds of both chambers, and Democrats have nowhere near two-thirds of either. In practice, the next two years will mostly be about oversight, must-pass spending deals, and messaging bills that set up 2028.

The first test comes before any of that. The Dec. 11 funding deadline falls inside the lame duck, so the outgoing Republican majority has to keep the government open while the incoming Democratic one decides how much leverage to save for January.

entry.title: The 2026 midterms: what happened, and where it was decided
entry.summary: Democrats took the House and Senate in a wave, but most seats were settled long before November. Here is the map before and after, the races decided in primaries, and the ones still being counted.
entry.content:
Democrats took both chambers of Congress on November 3, 2026, and it was not close. CBS News, NBC News and CNN all projected Democratic control of the House and the Senate before dawn on November 4.123 Counting is still under way, so every number below is a Wednesday-morning snapshot, not a certified result.

Chamber Before Nov 3 After Nov 3 (projected, Nov 4 morning) Still uncalled
Senate (100) 53 R, 47 D (45 D + 2 I) 54 D, 44 R 2 (Alaska, Mississippi)
House (435) 219 R, 214 D, 2 vacant D at least 258 (NBC); CBS estimates 259, range 251 to 268 about 53 to 75
Governors (36 up) GOP held a majority nationally Democrats flipped 5 (TX, GA, NV, OH, IA) 2 (Alaska, Kansas)

The Senate flipped on seven Republican-held seats and zero Democratic losses: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.4 In the House, no sitting Democrat lost, and mid-decade Republican redistricting in Texas, Florida, Missouri, North Carolina and Ohio did not stop the wave.5

Voters treated the election as a referendum on President Trump and on prices. CBS exit polls put his approval at 38 percent among midterm voters, with about nine in ten calling the cost of living a major or crucial factor, and majorities saying his tariffs hurt the economy and that military action against Iran was the wrong decision.65 Vice President Vance’s own verdict, quoted by CBS: “The reason we lost is the war.”7

The leadership fallout started within hours. Speaker Mike Johnson told his staff he will not seek the minority leader job, and Jim Jordan wants it. Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the House, and John Thune is expected to run for Senate minority leader.2

The Senate: 53 to 47 Republican becomes 54 to 44 Democratic

Thirty-five seats were on the ballot: the 33 regular seats plus special elections in Ohio (JD Vance’s old seat) and Florida (Marco Rubio’s). Republicans were defending 22 of them and Democrats 13.8 Democrats needed a net gain of four to take the chamber. They got seven, and gave back none.

The seven flips, in order of the call (vote shares from Fox News at 11:50 AM ET; call times from CBS):97

  • North Carolina (8:30 PM): Roy Cooper (D) 58.7, Michael Whatley (R) 39.1. The former governor becomes the state’s first Democratic senator in almost two decades. Open seat; Thom Tillis retired.
  • South Carolina (10:03 PM): Annie Andrews (D) 51.1, Darline Graham (R) 46.7. Lindsey Graham died on July 11. Gov. McMaster appointed his sister Darline at Trump’s recommendation, and she won a special GOP primary before losing to Andrews, a pediatrician and the first woman South Carolina has elected to the Senate.23 Cook had rated the seat Solid Republican in June.
  • Texas (10:59 PM): James Talarico (D) 55.1, Ken Paxton (R) 43.0. Trump endorsed Paxton over Sen. John Cornyn in the primary. Talarico’s win is the first statewide GOP loss in Texas in more than 30 years.2
  • Ohio special (11:15 PM): Sherrod Brown (D) 50.0, Jon Husted (R) 45.2. Brown returns two years after losing Ohio’s other seat.
  • Kansas (11:29 PM): Adam Hamilton (D) 50.9, Roger Marshall (R) 46.1. Kansas elected a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1932.24
  • Iowa (11:47 PM): Josh Turek (D) 50.5, Ashley Hinson (R) 46.4. Open seat; Joni Ernst retired. CBS tied the result to affordability and tariffs.
  • Maine (12:52 AM): Troy Jackson (D) 53.6, Susan Collins (R) 46.3. Collins’s 30-year run ends.

Democratic holds that had been rated competitive: Georgia (Ossoff 59.0 over Mike Collins 41.0), New Hampshire (Pappas 56.2 over John Sununu 42.0, open seat), Michigan (El-Sayed 52.5 over Mike Rogers 45.5, open seat), Minnesota (Flanagan 53.7 over Tafoya 43.6, open seat). None was within 7 points.

Republican holds that got closer than expected: Louisiana (Julia Letlow 50.9 over Jamie Davis 49.1, after Letlow ousted Sen. Bill Cassidy in the GOP primary), the Florida special (Ashley Moody 50.9 over Angie Nixon 48.0), and Nebraska (Pete Ricketts 50.4 over independent Dan Osborn 43.7, not called until 4:02 AM).

Uncalled: Alaska (Peltola 48.2, Sullivan 47.9, with ranked-choice tabulation still to come) and Mississippi (Colom 48.95, Hyde-Smith 48.94, separated by 43 votes). Both are covered below.

The House: a five-seat GOP majority becomes a Democratic landslide

Republicans went into the night with 219 seats (counting Kevin Kiley, who left the party but caucused with them), Democrats with 214, and two vacancies.5 Democrats needed a net gain of three. By late Wednesday morning NBC’s tracker had them at 236 called seats to 146, with 53 uncalled and 31 flips so far, and its model projected a final total of at least 258. CBS’s estimate was 259, in a range of 251 to 268.105

Who lost. Wikipedia’s running tally counts 26 Republican incumbents defeated plus Kiley, and 10 Republican open seats taken by Democrats. No Democratic incumbent lost.11 CBS’s list of defeated Republicans includes:5

  • Pennsylvania, four seats: Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-1, to Bob Harvie), Ryan Mackenzie (PA-7, Bob Brooks), Rob Bresnahan (PA-8, Paige Cognetti) and Scott Perry (PA-10, Janelle Stelson, in a rematch). Fitzpatrick had won by nearly 13 points in 2024.
  • Iowa, all three GOP seats: Mariannette Miller-Meeks (IA-1, Christina Bohannan, in their third rematch), the open IA-2 (Lindsay James) and Zach Nunn (IA-3, Sarah Trone Garriott).
  • Wisconsin, two: Bryan Steil (WI-1, Mitchell Berman) and Derrick Van Orden (WI-3, Rebecca Cooke).
  • Ohio, two: Max Miller (OH-7, Brian Poindexter), who stayed in the race after domestic-abuse allegations he denied, and Mike Carey (OH-15, Don Leonard).
  • Elsewhere: Tom Kean Jr. (NJ-7, Rebecca Bennett), Gabe Evans (CO-8, Manny Rutinel), Jen Kiggans (VA-2, Elaine Luria), Ann Wagner (MO-2, Fred Wellman), Victoria Spartz (IN-5, J.D. Ford), Monica De La Cruz (TX-15, Bobby Pulido), James Gallagher (CA-1, Mike McGuire), Kiley (CA-6, Richard Pan) and David Valadao (CA-22, Randy Villegas, projected by NBC).10 Mike Lawler (NY-17) conceded to Cait Conley at 2:45 AM, though the race was still formally uncalled because of ballot-scanner problems in Westchester.
  • Open seats that flipped: NC-11 (Jamie Ager, the first Democrat since 2010), KY-6 (Zach Dembo), NE-2 (Denise Powell), TX-23 (Katy Padilla Stout), TX-35 (Johnny Garcia), UT-1 (Ben McAdams, in a court-ordered district) and MI-10 (Christina Hines).

Redistricting did not save the majority. Seven Republican-run states redrew maps mid-decade to target about 15 Democratic seats.5 The results:

State What the new map tried to do What happened
Texas Make 5 seats more Republican Democrats flipped TX-15, TX-23 and TX-35, held TX-28 (Cuellar, 65.8 percent) and TX-34 (Gonzalez, 55.6), and led in redrawn TX-32
Florida Redraw 4 Democratic seats Castor (FL-14), Moskowitz (FL-25, 51.3 to 46.6) and the open FL-22 (Pia Dandiya) all held; 5 Florida seats still uncalled
North Carolina Make NC-1 more Republican Don Davis led Laurie Buckhout 50.1 to 46.8 with 99 percent in; uncalled
Alabama Court cleared a GOP-favored map Shomari Figures held AL-2
Missouri New 2025 map Voters rejected the map in a referendum, Proposition A, 62 to 38; Democrats flipped MO-2
Ohio Required redraw Kaptur held OH-9 (52.7 to 47.3); Democrats flipped OH-7 and OH-15
California Democrats countered by redrawing 5 GOP seats Democrats flipped CA-1, CA-6 and CA-22; 9 California seats uncalled
Utah Court-ordered map with one Democratic-leaning seat McAdams flipped UT-1

The Democratic Women’s Caucus said more than 100 Democratic women were elected, up from 97, a first for the group. Colorado’s Melat Kiros, 29, becomes the first Gen Z woman in Congress after beating Rep. Diana DeGette in the July primary.5

Decided before November

Most of the map was never in play. Of the 35 Senate races, Cook rated 22 as Solid for one party going in, and 23 ended up decided by 10 points or more.89 In those states, the real election was the primary.

Senate seats where the primary was the contest:

  • Texas: Ken Paxton beat Sen. John Cornyn in the May 26 Republican runoff by more than 25 points after Trump endorsed him on May 19. Cornyn had led the March 3 first round.25 Paxton then lost the general by 12. Here the primary chose the nominee but did not settle the seat.
  • Louisiana: Rep. Julia Letlow, with Trump’s endorsement, knocked out Sen. Bill Cassidy in the state’s first closed party primary since 2010 (May 16: Letlow 44.8, John Fleming 28.3, Cassidy 24.8), then won the June 27 runoff with 56.9 percent. Forecasters called the seat safe, and Letlow held it by 1.8 points.26
  • Kentucky: Rep. Andy Barr took 60.5 percent in the May 19 GOP primary over former Attorney General Daniel Cameron for Mitch McConnell’s open seat, then won 55.0 to 42.9 over Charles Booker.27
  • Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed won the August 4 Democratic primary with 48.5 percent over Rep. Haley Stevens after Mallory McMorrow withdrew. Mike Rogers was the only Republican to qualify.28
  • Safe open seats settled in spring: Alabama (Barry Moore, 54.7), Montana (Kurt Alme, 49.0 over independent Seth Bodnar 37.3), Oklahoma (Kevin Hern, 57.3), Wyoming (Harriet Hageman, 65.2), Illinois (Juliana Stratton, 61.0) and Minnesota (Peggy Flanagan, 53.7).9
  • Kansas: Adam Hamilton won an eight-way Democratic primary with just 34.6 percent, then beat Sen. Roger Marshall.24

House seats with no real general election. 270toWin counts 18 districts with only one major party on the November ballot, down from 37 in 2024:12

  • Entirely unopposed (5): FL-10 Maxwell Frost, MA-2 Jim McGovern, MA-5 Katherine Clark, MA-7 Ayanna Pressley, WI-2 Mark Pocan.
  • No major-party opponent (4): LA-2 Troy Carter, MA-1 Richard Neal, NJ-8 Rob Menendez, PA-3 (open, won by Chris Rabb).
  • Same-party California top-two races (9): CA-4, CA-7, CA-11 (Pelosi’s open seat), CA-12, CA-14, CA-29, CA-34, CA-37, and CA-40, where Republicans Young Kim and Ken Calvert faced each other.

Primaries that ended House careers. Eleven incumbents lost renomination, 7 Democrats and 4 Republicans.1311 In safe seats, that primary was the election:

District Incumbent out Who beat them Storyline
CO-1 Diana DeGette (D) Melat Kiros Democratic socialist, 29; won the general with 78 percent
NY-13 Adriano Espaillat (D) Darializa Avila Chevalier Democratic socialist, backed by Mayor Mamdani
NY-10 Dan Goldman (D) Brad Lander Former NYC comptroller, Mamdani-backed
MI-13 Shri Thanedar (D) Donavan McKinney DSA-backed state rep
CT-1 John Larson (D) Luke Bronin Former Hartford mayor
TX-18 Al Green (D) Christian Menefee Incumbent vs. incumbent after the Texas redraw
TX-33 Julie Johnson (D) Colin Allred Former congressman, runoff
KY-4 Thomas Massie (R) Ed Gallrein Trump-backed; about $37M, the costliest House primary ever
TN-5 Andy Ogles (R) Charlie Hatcher Lost despite Trump’s endorsement
TX-2 Dan Crenshaw (R) Steve Toth Toth then held the seat only 51 to 49
FL-7 Cory Mills (R) Primary loss The open seat was still uncalled Wednesday

Sixty House members retired or ran for something else (26 Democrats, 36 Republicans), the second-most in any cycle since 1992.11

The close ones

Twelve Senate races finished inside 10 points, and two are still being counted.

Mississippi: 43 votes. With about 96 percent counted, Scott Colom (D) led Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith 462,821 to 462,778.1415 Colom’s campaign says 10,000 to 15,000 affidavit ballots remain, and Hyde-Smith’s says its numbers show her winning. Mississippi has no automatic or candidate-requested recount, so any challenge goes to court. Colom says he is prepared to go there.2 Cook had rated the seat Likely Republican.

Alaska: 0.3 points and a name on the ballot. Mary Peltola (D) led Sen. Dan Sullivan 102,701 to 102,075 in first choices, with Republican Gerald Heikes at 4,821 and an undeclared retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan at 3,583.16 Tens of thousands of ballots were uncounted. Ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18 and certification for November 25. The Trump administration sued to block certification over voter confusion with the namesake candidate, and a federal judge dismissed the suit without a hearing. The DOJ, FBI and state police opened investigations into reports that Democratic operatives recruited him; Peltola and the DSCC deny it. Spending topped $100 million, against $28 million in 2020. Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal ranked-choice voting, was itself too close to call at 48 to 52.17

The money. AdImpact projected a record $11.6 billion in political ads this cycle.18 By OpenSecrets’ method, counting candidate plus outside spending as of October 23, Texas became the most expensive Senate race ever at about $560 million, passing the $516 million Georgia 2020-21 runoff. Ohio was at $423 million, Michigan $337 million, Iowa $185 million, Georgia $179 million, Maine $172 million, North Carolina $131 million and Alaska $130 million.19 Talarico’s victory line, “Texas is not for sale,” was aimed at Elon Musk’s reported $150 million-plus for Paxton.7 In the House, AdImpact put NC-1 (Don Davis vs. Laurie Buckhout) over $52 million, the most expensive House race in history, followed by FL-25, MI-7, NY-17, MI-10, TX-34, WI-3, CO-8, FL-14 and CA-22.20

NBC listed 53 House seats uncalled at midday, including 9 in California, 5 each in Arizona and Florida, and 4 each in Texas and New York.10 Western states that vote by mail will take days, and CNN warned official results could take weeks.3

Heated for reasons beyond the margin: Texas (Musk money, Paxton’s scandals, a 30-year streak ending), Alaska (the namesake candidate and federal investigations), South Carolina (a sister appointed to her late brother’s seat), Ohio’s Max Miller (abuse allegations), New Jersey’s Tom Kean Jr. (months of missed votes during undisclosed depression treatment), and Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn held Pete Ricketts under 51 percent.

Governors and ballot measures

Governors. Democrats flipped Texas (Gina Hinojosa 52.8 over Gov. Greg Abbott 45.7, ending 30 years of GOP control), Georgia (Keisha Lance Bottoms 54.3 over Rick Jackson), Nevada (Aaron Ford 51.7 over Gov. Joe Lombardo), Ohio (Amy Acton 52.3 over Vivek Ramaswamy 44.4) and Iowa (Rob Sand 55.5 over Zach Lahn). They now hold a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years.222 Alaska (Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, D, leading) and Kansas (Cindy Holscher, D, 50.26 to Ty Masterson 49.74) were uncalled.

The closest governor races were Kansas (0.5), Florida (1.3, Byron Donalds over David Jolly), Tennessee (2.5, Marsha Blackburn over Jerri Green), New Hampshire (4.0, Kelly Ayotte), Alabama (4.1, Tommy Tuberville over Doug Jones) and South Carolina (4.5, Alan Wilson).22

Two patterns stand out. Voter ID and citizenship requirements passed everywhere they were called, often in the same states that elected Democrats. And Missouri voters both rejected the legislature’s mid-decade congressional map and refused to roll back the abortion rights they approved in 2024.

entry.title: The deadliest weather in America doesn't come with a siren
entry.summary: Tornadoes get the headlines. Across nearly three decades of NOAA records, heat has killed almost three times as many people.
entry.content:
Ask someone to name the deadliest kind of severe weather and most people will say tornadoes. That makes sense: tornadoes are sudden, violent, and easy to film. But the records tell a different story.

NOAA’s Storm Events Database has tracked the full range of weather hazards since 1996. Since then it has recorded 22,713 deaths. Heat and excessive heat account for 6,313 of them, about 28%. Tornadoes account for 2,176.

Interactive chart: Deaths by event type, 1996–2024 — view it on What Works? →

It’s getting worse, or we’re counting better, or both

Heat deaths in the database have climbed sharply. From 2015 to 2024 NOAA recorded 3,666 of them, nearly triple the 1,321 recorded from 2005 to 2014. The worst year on record was 2023, with 879.

Interactive chart: Heat deaths per year — view it on What Works? →

One caveat applies here. A death only appears in this database if it gets attributed to a weather event, and attribution practices vary across places and over time. Some of this rise reflects better counting. Even so, the trend is consistent with what public-health agencies have been reporting.

Where and when

Heat deaths cluster where you’d expect: the desert Southwest and the peak of summer. July alone accounts for more than half of them.

Interactive chart: Heat deaths by state, 1996–2024 — view it on What Works? →

Interactive chart: Heat deaths by month — view it on What Works? →

What works

Unlike a tornado, a heat wave arrives with days of warning, which makes most heat deaths preventable. The approaches public-health agencies point to are simple ones. They include cooling centers people can actually reach, checking on neighbors who live alone, keeping water and shade available for outdoor workers, and treating heat warnings with the same seriousness as a tornado warning.

Want to dig in yourself? Every number in this story comes from the Storm Desk. Switch the event type to “Heat” to see the rest.

entry.title: Welcome to the What Works? News Center
entry.summary: Everyday solutions, out-of-the-ordinary situations, and the news behind both, now with a newsroom.
entry.content:
What Works? started as a channel about everyday solutions and fresh takes on out-of-the-ordinary situations. This site is where that work comes together. Videos and clips from YouTube and Twitch sit alongside written reporting on politics, economics, technology and science.

Here’s what you’ll find:

  • From the Channel: new videos and the best Twitch clips, each with a write-up.
  • Politics & Economics: policy and markets, judged by one question: does it work?
  • Technology & Science: explained plainly by someone with a computer science degree who likes reading the primary source.
  • The Storm Desk: an explorable archive of 75 years of NOAA storm records, plus stories built from it.

Start with the Storm Desk, or read our first data story on the deadliest weather in America.
